title: The meter that never looks at the gate

data.source: Blackwell (1948); the renewal-reward theorem (textbook, Ross 1970); Birkhoff (1931); cited from memory. Simulated R4 rotor with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck force, seeded.

prediction: Cuts per unit time are v/a, surplus per unit time is mean surplus over mean gap and equals twice the mean backward speed over sigma, the same for a = pi and a = pi/3; Blackwell's theorem holds for the noisy rotor and does not apply to the printed noise-free one.
baseline: The renewal-reward theorem (Ross 1970), the ergodic theorem (Birkhoff 1931) and Blackwell's renewal theorem (1948). Decoy: twice the share of time spent moving backward, times v over sigma.
relation: identical to the renewal-reward ratio; the long-run surplus rate needs no cut
status_line: CRR here is: a renaming of the renewal-reward ratio; and the long-run surplus per unit time does not depend on where the cuts fall.
why: The long-run rates of cuts and of surplus are the renewal-reward ratio, to the tolerances written down. The surplus per unit time came out the same when the cut distance was made three times shorter: it is twice the mean backward speed over the ruler, a property of the force eta (Phoenix R4, ASSUMPTION; erratum 1) and not of the cut (R2, ASSUMPTION). Blackwell's theorem needs gaps that are random; the printed noise-free rotor has two fixed gaps and its window count never settles.
